title: Shaders & Rendering
notes: What work must happen before an asset becomes visible pixels? That is our central rendering question. Ned will explain how triangle data becomes a rendered image. Our Unreal examples let us trace specific parts of that process: texture sampling and color, vertex motion in water, and lighting or stylized shading. For each example, identify the input, the operation, and where it belongs in the pipeline. Today we explain behavior and form testable cost predictions; next week we measure them.

title: Real-time rendering: scene data to pixels
notes: Use this as our map for the rest of class. CPU-side scene logic and draw preparation submit work using mesh, material and texture data. Vertex processing transforms positions and supplies attributes. Primitive assembly and clipping prepare triangles for rasterization. Rasterization determines covered samples; attributes such as UVs and normals are interpolated for shading. Fragment or pixel shading uses those inputs and texture samples. Depth/stencil tests and blending govern contributions to render targets; lighting and post-processing can involve additional passes before presentation. Depth tests can happen early, so this is a logical orientation rather than a rigid timing diagram. In our Unreal examples, World Position Offset affects vertex positions. Texture flow changes sampling coordinates, and Base Color is an input to surface shading, not the final screen color. More objects, vertices, shaded samples or memory traffic are possible sources of work, not proof of the measured bottleneck.

title: Coordinates tell the shader where to look
notes: If a checker texture becomes stretched on part of a mesh, inspect the UV mapping before blaming texture resolution. UVs are sampling addresses; local and world positions are different coordinate frames. A direction is not a position: translation affects points, not direction vectors. Unreal distinguishes Transform from TransformPosition. Compare vectors in the same space. For this class the texture-flow lesson changes UVs, while World Position Offset changes geometry. Those are different mechanisms even when both suggest moving water.

title: Normals and dot products: predict the signal
notes: A normal describes surface orientation; normalizing is an operation that makes a nonzero vector length one. These are different ideas. For unit vectors the dot product is the cosine of their angle: one for matching directions, zero at a right angle, and minus one for opposite directions. Unreal world Up is positive Z. A sideways-facing normal has zero dot with Up. This same reasoning will drive our light bands and view-angle edges. Normalize both inputs and put them in the same coordinate space. Reversing a cross product reverses its direction, which matters when constructing normals from triangle edges. Do not normalize a zero vector as a direction. Which faces would a positive world-Up mask select?

title: Rendering work and frame budgets
notes: These are categories for a hypothesis, not a ranking of our materials. Many objects and draws can increase CPU submission work. Mesh density and deformation affect vertex work. Screen coverage, repeated shading and texture samples can affect pixel work. Meshes, textures and render targets occupy memory; accessing or moving their data creates traffic. Capacity is how much can be stored, latency is how long an access takes, and bandwidth is the rate at which data can be transferred. These distinctions replace no hardware experiment today; the optional table is a map for later investigation. In the pre-assessment example, CPU time is nine milliseconds and GPU time is twenty-four. Their work can overlap, so do not simply add them. At 60 FPS, the frame budget is about 16.7 milliseconds and the GPU exceeds it. Use pass timings to select a controlled test; node count or a changed parameter value alone does not establish frame cost.
